items.prompt: A company needs 300 employees to access 25 AWS accounts with job-based permissions. Employees already have accounts in a corporate identity provider. Which AWS design best centralizes workforce access?
constraints: The employees are human workforce identities, not application workloads.
The company wants group-based assignments across many AWS accounts.
The company wants to avoid creating and rotating separate IAM users in every account.

options.text: Use an AWS Organizations organization instance of IAM Identity Center, connect the corporate identity source, and assign permission sets to groups and accounts.
Create one IAM user per employee in every account and copy the same password policy to all accounts.
Create one root user per employee and place the root passwords in the corporate directory.
Give every employee the same IAM access key and use the employee's workstation name for attribution.

feedback.Reason: IAM Identity Center is designed to centralize workforce access to multiple AWS accounts through groups, assignments, and permission sets.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: An organization instance of IAM Identity Center provides a central place to assign workforce users and groups to AWS accounts with permission sets. It can connect an existing identity provider and avoids per-account IAM-user administration for workforce access.
Details.scenarioApplication: The company can synchronize or connect its corporate identities, assign job-based permission sets to groups and accounts, and give employees portal access to the accounts they need.
Details.errorCorrection: IAM users per account create duplicated lifecycle work, while root credentials and shared keys destroy least privilege and individual attribution.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Permission-set design still requires least privilege and periodic review; centralization reduces duplication but does not make broad permissions safe.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Per-account IAM users multiply provisioning, deprovisioning, password, and audit work across 25 accounts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root users are account-level emergency identities, not workforce identities, and must not be distributed to employees.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A shared access key provides no reliable individual attribution and is a long-term secret.

items.prompt: A platform team enabled IAM Identity Center separately in each member account, but wants one place to manage employee access to all accounts. Which change addresses the architecture?
constraints: The accounts belong to one AWS Organization.
The company wants organization-wide account assignments.
There is no requirement to isolate IAM Identity Center to a single application account.

options.text: Use an organization instance of IAM Identity Center in the Organizations management account and manage account assignments centrally.
Keep every account instance and synchronize them by sharing the root password among account administrators.
Replace IAM Identity Center with an EC2 instance that stores a copy of every employee's access key.
Create an account instance in the management account and assume it automatically controls all member accounts.

feedback.Reason: Only an organization instance provides the central multi-account workforce access model described.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM Identity Center supports organization and account instances. An organization instance is deployed in the Organizations management account and manages access to AWS accounts across the organization; account instances are bound to individual accounts and have narrower use cases.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team should select the organization instance model and consolidate workforce assignments rather than maintaining independent account-level access stores.
Details.errorCorrection: Account instances do not automatically synchronize or control other accounts, and root passwords or stored access keys are not federation mechanisms.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: An account instance can be appropriate for an isolated application use case, but the stated organization-wide account access requires the organization instance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Independent account instances remain separate control planes; sharing root credentials is unsafe and does not synchronize access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An EC2 credential store would create long-term secret distribution and no native workforce assignment model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An account instance is bound to its account and does not become an organization-wide access manager automatically.

items.prompt: An organization wants some employees managed in IAM Identity Center and others managed by an external IdP, with both sources assigning access to the same AWS accounts. What limitation must the architect include in the design?
constraints: The organization uses one IAM Identity Center organization instance.
Both populations would need the same account-assignment mechanism.
The company has not chosen to create separate AWS Organizations.

options.text: IAM Identity Center supports only one identity source per organization, so the organization must choose and integrate one authoritative source.
IAM Identity Center supports unlimited identity sources as long as each source uses a different password policy.
The organization should use the account root user as a neutral identity source for both populations.
The organization should create duplicate users in every source and rely on matching display names.

feedback.Reason: An IAM Identity Center organization has one configured identity source, so the workforce directory architecture must establish one authoritative source for that instance.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The identity source defines where IAM Identity Center users and groups are managed. AWS documents one identity source per organization, with choices including an external IdP or users and groups managed directly in IAM Identity Center.
Details.scenarioApplication: The organization must consolidate or federate the required populations into the chosen source, or separate the populations into a different account and organization boundary if that is truly required.
Details.errorCorrection: Password policies and display-name matching do not create separate authoritative identity sources, and root is not a workforce directory.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Choosing an external IdP centralizes workforce lifecycle and existing controls, while native IAM Identity Center users reduce dependencies but still require lifecycle ownership.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The organization instance has one identity source; multiple password policies do not change that control-plane limit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The root user is an AWS account identity, not a directory or identity source for employees.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Duplicate users create lifecycle and attribution drift; matching display names do not establish identity authority.

items.prompt: A company already uses a SAML 2.0 identity provider for employees and wants one federation point for access to multiple AWS accounts and supported AWS applications. Which service best fits?
constraints: The company wants to keep the external IdP as the workforce authority.
The organization wants central account assignments rather than separate IAM roles configured manually in every account.
The company can configure the IdP integration and provisioning path.

options.text: Integrate the IdP with an organization instance of IAM Identity Center and use its account assignments and permission sets.
Create a separate SAML provider and hand-authored role trust policy in every account, with no central assignment layer.
Use an S3 bucket policy as the SAML federation endpoint for employee sessions.
Create one IAM user for the IdP and share its access key with every employee.

feedback.Reason: IAM Identity Center provides a central federation point and multi-account assignment model for workforce users connected to an external IdP.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM Identity Center can connect an existing identity provider and lets administrators assign permission sets to users or groups for AWS accounts. SAML 2.0 is a supported federation technology, while the service centralizes the account-access workflow.
Details.scenarioApplication: The IdP remains authoritative for workforce authentication, and IAM Identity Center owns the account and permission-set assignments rather than duplicating hand-authored federation roles in every account.
Details.errorCorrection: Direct SAML federation can be valid for a bounded use case, but it leaves the stated multi-account assignment problem to repeated account configuration; S3 policies and IAM users are not federation endpoints.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A legacy single-account integration may still use direct SAML federation, but the organization-wide workforce use case favors the centralized Identity Center pattern.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Direct per-account SAML configuration duplicates the control plane and does not supply the central assignment model requested.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 bucket policies authorize S3 resource requests and are not SAML federation endpoints.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A shared IAM-user key is a long-term credential with no individual workforce attribution.

items.prompt: A corporate IdP must automatically provision users and groups into IAM Identity Center so administrators can assign them to AWS accounts. Which integration addresses that lifecycle need?
constraints: The IdP supports the SCIM protocol.
The company wants provisioning changes to flow from the IdP rather than manual CSV imports.
IAM Identity Center remains the account-assignment control plane.

options.text: Configure automatic provisioning with SCIM from the external IdP to IAM Identity Center, then manage account assignments in Identity Center.
Put the IdP administrator password in every IAM role trust policy so the roles can create users.
Use an S3 event notification to copy employee passwords into IAM Identity Center.
Create one access key for the HR system and use it as every employee's AWS identity.

feedback.Reason: SCIM provides the documented automatic provisioning path from a supported external IdP into IAM Identity Center.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM Identity Center supports automatic provisioning of users and groups from an external identity provider using SCIM. The provisioned identities can then be used for account and application assignments.
Details.scenarioApplication: The IdP remains the lifecycle source, SCIM synchronizes the identities, and IAM Identity Center controls which groups receive which permission sets in which accounts.
Details.errorCorrection: Trust policies do not store IdP passwords, S3 notifications are not identity provisioning, and a shared access key cannot represent individual employees.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Provisioning synchronization must be monitored for errors and attribute mapping; SCIM does not replace permission-set review or IdP authentication controls.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Passwords must not be distributed through role trust policies, and trust policies do not provision workforce identities.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 event notifications do not provide a secure workforce identity provisioning protocol.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A shared key loses individual identity and creates a long-term secret with broad lifecycle impact.

items.prompt: An employee leaves the company. The employee is disabled in the corporate IdP, but the corresponding IAM Identity Center user still appears assigned to a production account. Which control should the architect verify first?
constraints: The organization uses SCIM provisioning from the IdP.
The employee must lose workforce access promptly.
The organization wants the source directory to remain authoritative.

options.text: Verify SCIM deprovisioning and synchronization health, then remove or disable the user's account assignments according to the offboarding procedure.
Leave the assignment in place because disabling the IdP account automatically changes every AWS role policy.
Rotate the account root password because it controls employee assignments.
Delete all permission sets so no former employee can use the account.

feedback.Reason: Offboarding must be verified across the authoritative IdP, SCIM synchronization, and IAM Identity Center account assignments.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SCIM synchronizes user and group lifecycle data, while IAM Identity Center assignments determine which users or groups can access accounts. A failure in either synchronization or assignment removal can leave an effective access path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team should inspect the synchronization status and explicit assignment, remediate the stale path, and preserve the IdP as the authoritative lifecycle source.
Details.errorCorrection: Disabling an IdP account is not evidence that every downstream assignment or session has already been revoked, and root credentials do not manage employee offboarding.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Existing sessions and cached portal credentials may require additional session and revocation controls; the offboarding process should define those timing expectations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An IdP disable event does not prove that synchronization and account assignments are healthy or that existing sessions are gone.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root password rotation is unrelated to workforce account assignments.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting permission sets is destructive and would affect active employees; remove the specific user's access instead.

items.prompt: An architect creates a `ReadOnlyOperations` permission set and assigns it to a group in three accounts. What does IAM Identity Center create or manage in the target accounts?
constraints: The assignment is successful.
The permission set contains the intended policies.
The architect is not manually creating a separate IAM user in each account.

options.text: IAM Identity Center creates corresponding Identity Center-controlled IAM roles in the assigned accounts and attaches the permission-set policies to those roles.
IAM Identity Center copies the employee's root credentials into each account.
IAM Identity Center creates one permanent IAM access key that all group members share.
The permission set is only a local browser bookmark and does not produce an AWS authorization role.

feedback.Reason: Permission-set assignments produce IAM Identity Center-controlled roles in the target accounts, which users assume through the access portal or CLI.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A permission set is a reusable template containing policies. When assigned to a user or group in an account, IAM Identity Center creates and manages the corresponding role and keeps its policies aligned with the permission set.
Details.scenarioApplication: The group members receive the `ReadOnlyOperations` role session in each assigned account, with no per-user long-term key distribution.
Details.errorCorrection: Permission sets are an authorization template and role-management mechanism, not a root-secret or shared-access-key distribution service.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The managed role should not be edited as an independent long-term customization path; changes should be made through the permission set and assignment model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Root credentials are never copied to workforce users or accounts as part of permission-set assignment.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM Identity Center uses role sessions and does not create a shared permanent access key for the group.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A permission set is an AWS authorization template that results in managed roles in assigned accounts.

items.prompt: All members of the `DataAnalysts` group need read-only access to two analytics accounts, while only the `DataPlatform` group needs a write permission set in one account. Which assignment is most maintainable?
constraints: The groups are synchronized from the authoritative workforce directory.
The analyst and platform permissions are different.
The company wants membership changes to update access without editing every person individually.

options.text: Assign the read-only permission set to `DataAnalysts` in both accounts and the write permission set to `DataPlatform` only in the required account.
Assign administrator access to every user and rely on group names for documentation only.
Create one shared IAM user for both groups and change its password when membership changes.
Assign the write permission set to both groups because read-only users may need future access.

feedback.Reason: IAM Identity Center assignments can bind a group and a permission set to the exact accounts where that access is needed.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Account assignments associate users or groups with permission sets and target AWS accounts. Group-based assignments make directory membership the lifecycle control while keeping permission sets reusable and scoped.
Details.scenarioApplication: The analyst group receives only its read-only role in both accounts, and the platform group receives the write role only where required.
Details.errorCorrection: Administrator access and shared users erase the group-specific authorization boundary; possible future needs do not justify present write access.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A user in multiple groups may receive multiple permission sets, so the combined effective access should be reviewed for least privilege.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Group membership cannot make an administrator policy least privilege; the permission set must express the actual job access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Shared IAM users destroy individual attribution and create a fragile password lifecycle.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Future access is not a current requirement; assigning write access to analysts violates least privilege.

items.prompt: A workforce user is assigned a permission set with a one-hour AWS-account session duration. The team asks to make the user stay signed into the account for 24 hours by changing only the portal session duration. What should the architect explain?
constraints: The permission set session duration remains one hour.
The portal session can be configured independently.
The user needs authorization to the account, not merely an open browser tab.

options.text: The portal session and AWS-account session are separate; the account role session is still bounded by the permission set's configured duration and its maximum.
The portal session duration always overrides the permission-set role session duration.
The user should use a root access key because portal sessions cannot expire.
The permission set duration controls only the IdP password age and has no effect on AWS access.

feedback.Reason: IAM Identity Center has distinct portal and AWS-account session durations; extending one does not override the other.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The permission-set session duration controls how long a user is signed into the assigned AWS account role, with documented bounds. The AWS access portal session duration controls portal authentication separately.
Details.scenarioApplication: The user must re-establish the account role session after one hour unless the permission set is changed within the allowed maximum; a longer portal session alone does not grant an active account session.
Details.errorCorrection: Portal authentication and account authorization are different sessions, and root keys are not a way to bypass session policy.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Longer account sessions reduce reauthentication interruptions but extend the exposure window of a workforce session; the duration should match the task and risk.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The portal session does not override the permission set's AWS-account session duration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root keys are unrelated to IAM Identity Center session duration and must not be used for workforce access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Permission-set session duration directly controls the account role session, not the IdP password age.

items.prompt: An administrator has both `ReadOnlyOperations` and `AdministratorAccess` permission sets assigned. Which daily-use behavior best follows least privilege?
constraints: The daily task is log review and configuration inspection.
No production mutation is required for the task.
Both permission sets appear in the AWS access portal.

options.text: Choose the `ReadOnlyOperations` account role in the AWS access portal and use the administrative role only for an approved task that requires it.
Choose `AdministratorAccess` every time because the user is eligible for it.
Use the root user for inspection so the read-only permission set is never exercised.
Share the administrator portal session with the rest of the team so fewer users need assignments.

feedback.Reason: IAM Identity Center exposes assigned permission sets as account roles, allowing the user to choose the least-privilege role for each task.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Each assigned permission set appears as an available role in the AWS access portal. AWS guidance recommends choosing the most restrictive permission set that can perform the task rather than remaining in an administrative session.
Details.scenarioApplication: The administrator inspects logs through the read-only role and elevates only when the operational contract requires a change.
Details.errorCorrection: Eligibility for an administrative role is not a reason to use it for every task, and root or shared sessions defeat individual attribution.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A separate elevation path adds a step but reduces the blast radius of routine session compromise and makes the intended privilege boundary visible.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Using the broadest role by default violates the stated least-privilege goal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The root user is not a daily inspection identity and would enlarge rather than reduce risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Sharing a portal session destroys individual attribution and expands access beyond assigned users.

items.prompt: A customer has one AWS account and an existing SAML 2.0 IdP. It needs employees to sign in to the AWS console by receiving temporary credentials for approved IAM roles, but it does not need centralized multi-account assignments. Which option is a valid fit?
constraints: The customer can configure the IdP metadata and IAM SAML provider.
The customer will keep role trust and permissions policies narrowly scoped.
There is no requirement for IAM Identity Center account assignments.

options.text: Use direct SAML 2.0 federation with an IAM SAML identity provider and roles in the account.
Create an IAM user for every employee and make the IdP send each user's password to IAM.
Use an S3 presigned URL as the console federation assertion.
Use the root user as the SAML service provider so IAM role policies are unnecessary.

feedback.Reason: Direct SAML federation is a valid bounded workforce-access pattern when an external IdP issues assertions for IAM roles and centralized Identity Center account assignment is not required.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM supports SAML 2.0 federation in which an external identity provider authenticates the user and AWS issues temporary credentials for an allowed IAM role. The role trust and permissions policies remain separate controls.
Details.scenarioApplication: The single-account customer can configure its IdP and IAM SAML provider, then constrain which roles the assertion may request and what those roles can do.
Details.errorCorrection: SAML federation does not require or justify copying passwords into IAM, and S3 URLs or root users are not federation mechanisms.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Direct federation can create more per-account configuration work as the estate grows; if multi-account central assignment becomes a requirement, IAM Identity Center becomes the stronger control plane.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: IAM does not receive workforce passwords from the IdP as an IAM-user provisioning pattern, and it creates unnecessary long-term identities.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A presigned URL grants access to an S3 object and is not a SAML assertion or console federation protocol.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The root user is not a SAML service provider and does not eliminate IAM role authorization.

items.prompt: An application running on EC2 must join a managed Microsoft Active Directory domain and use domain authentication. Which AWS service family addresses the directory infrastructure requirement?
constraints: The application needs an actual directory service for domain join and LDAP/Kerberos-compatible authentication.
The requirement is not merely AWS-account console access for administrators.
The team wants AWS-managed directory options rather than running domain controllers on EC2.

options.text: Use AWS Directory Service, selecting the directory type and connectivity model that matches the application's Microsoft AD requirements.
Use IAM Identity Center permission sets as a replacement for all application-domain authentication protocols.
Use an S3 bucket policy to create LDAP users for the application.
Use the account root user as the domain administrator for every application request.

feedback.Reason: AWS Directory Service provides managed directory options for workloads that require Microsoft AD-compatible domain services; IAM Identity Center solves a different workforce account-access problem.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS Directory Service offers directory types and integrations for applications that need directory protocols and domain capabilities. IAM Identity Center manages workforce access to AWS accounts and applications, not every application-domain authentication protocol.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect should select the Directory Service option that fits domain join, network connectivity, and managed-directory requirements, then separately design AWS permissions for the EC2 workload.
Details.errorCorrection: A permission set does not turn into an LDAP/Kerberos directory, and S3 policies or root credentials cannot provide domain services.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The directory choice affects compatibility, network placement, management responsibility, and cost; it should be driven by the application's protocol and trust requirements.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: IAM Identity Center is for workforce access to AWS accounts and applications, not a replacement for a managed Microsoft AD domain.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: S3 authorization does not create directory users or domain protocols.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Root credentials are unrelated to application domain authentication and should not be used by workloads.

items.prompt: A security team removes an unused action from a permission set. What is the canonical place to make that change so assigned accounts converge on the updated access?
constraints: The permission set is assigned to multiple accounts.
The team wants Identity Center to manage the corresponding account roles.
No account-specific exception is required.

options.text: Edit the permission set in IAM Identity Center, validate the change, and let Identity Center update the corresponding managed roles.
Edit the generated IAM role separately in every account and leave the permission set unchanged.
Edit the root user's policy because permission sets inherit all root permissions.
Ask each employee to remove the action from their browser session manually.

feedback.Reason: The permission set is the canonical managed template; editing it allows IAM Identity Center to update the corresponding roles and policies in assigned accounts.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM Identity Center manages roles created from permission sets and updates their policies when the permission set changes. The permission set is therefore the intended source of authorization configuration for that assignment.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team changes one permission set, reviews propagation and effective access, and avoids creating account-level drift by editing generated roles directly.
Details.errorCorrection: Direct edits to generated roles can be overwritten or diverge from the central template, and root or browser sessions do not own the permission-set policy.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A genuine account-specific exception may require a separate permission set or explicit architecture decision; silently editing generated roles would hide the ownership boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Editing generated roles independently creates drift and bypasses the permission-set control plane.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Root permissions are not inherited by permission sets, and root is not the policy owner for workforce assignments.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A browser session cannot modify the authorization template or reliably update other account roles.

items.prompt: A company wants all workforce users to satisfy the corporate MFA policy before reaching AWS accounts through IAM Identity Center. Where should the architect place the primary MFA control?
constraints: The external IdP is the authoritative workforce authentication system.
The company wants a consistent MFA policy across other corporate applications too.
AWS account assignments remain managed by IAM Identity Center.

options.text: Enforce the workforce MFA policy in the external IdP used as IAM Identity Center's identity source, and keep AWS account assignments in Identity Center.
Give every employee the root user's MFA device so AWS accounts share one second factor.
Put the corporate MFA password in each permission set as an IAM policy action.
Disable IdP MFA and rely on the permission set's read-only policy to protect stolen passwords.

feedback.Reason: When the external IdP is the workforce identity source, its authentication policy is the natural centralized MFA boundary for the employee population.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: IAM Identity Center connects workforce identities to AWS accounts and can use an external identity source. The identity provider authenticates the workforce user, while Identity Center controls which account roles and permission sets are available after authentication.
Details.scenarioApplication: The company enforces MFA once at the corporate IdP for the workforce and preserves Identity Center for group, account, and permission-set authorization.
Details.errorCorrection: Root MFA devices are account-specific and must not be shared, IAM policies do not store passwords or perform workforce authentication, and read-only access does not replace MFA.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The IdP-to-Identity-Center integration and session behavior must be tested end to end; AWS-native MFA requirements may still apply to separate IAM or root identities outside the workforce path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Sharing a root MFA device destroys individual attribution and violates root safeguards.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: IAM policies authorize actions; they do not contain a corporate password or implement an MFA challenge.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Read-only authorization limits post-authentication actions but does not protect the authentication event from password compromise.
